title: Weekly Briefing: Meta's AI Workforce Plan Implosion, Junior Tech Jobs Get Harder, and the Three-Year Degree Debate
author: Future Ready Leadership
summary: This week's Future Ready Leadership briefing synthesizes three stories under a single theme: the widening gap between organizations' AI ambitions and the trust and readiness needed to execute them. The lead story covers Reuters' reporting on Meta's abandoned "AI native" workforce plan, which explored cutting some teams by up to 60% before employee backlash, tanking internal sentiment, and weak productivity data forced Zuckerberg to cancel a second layoff wave hours before it began. The second item uses Business Insider and Axios data to show software engineering hiring is recovering unevenly — increasingly tilted toward senior roles who can judge AI-generated output — raising the risk that companies underinvest in the junior talent pipeline that produces future senior engineers. The third piece covers the spread of reduced-credit three-year bachelor's degrees across 26 states, framing it as employers and colleges both redefining what "workforce ready" credentials should look like. A closing podcast segment with WalkMe's Ofir Bloch adds a data point that undercuts AI optimism directly: employees now lose 51 working days a year to technology friction, up from 43 in 2024, even as their confidence in using AI tools stays high.
points: Meta's internal "Project OT" scenarios modeled cutting some teams by up to 60% for an AI-native workforce, but Zuckerberg called off a planned second layoff wave hours before it began after internal favorability dropped from 74% to 55% and AI-driven code changes didn't translate into shipped features.

Nearly 70% of U.S. software development job postings on Indeed in Q1 were for senior-level roles (up from 55% in 2019), suggesting AI is raising the bar for who gets hired rather than simply eliminating engineering jobs — with the risk that junior pipelines starve as a result.

BLS projections cited via Axios expect AI demand to help create 926,700 new professional/scientific/technical jobs while eliminating 752,100 office and administrative support roles, reframing "will AI kill jobs" as "which capabilities is the organization actually building."

26 U.S. states now have at least one reduced-credit, three-year bachelor's program (119 announced per RAND), forcing employers to get clearer about what a degree signals if the credential itself is being redefined.

WalkMe's 2026 data shows employees lose 51 working days a year to technology friction (up from 43 in 2024 and 36 in 2025) even though 90% feel confident using AI — evidence that the bottleneck is reliability at the point of work, not user confidence or tool access.
quotes: According to Reuters, internal scenarios explored cutting some teams by as much as 60%. Meta moved forward with a 10% reduction in May, but Mark Zuckerberg called off planning for a second wave just hours before the first layoffs began.

Internal sentiment dropped from 74% favorable to 55%, and internal data suggested the AI tools were not producing the productivity gains leaders hoped for. Code changes were up 220% year over year, but changes that led to new or upgraded features reaching users were only up 36%.

AI can help produce code, but someone still needs to know what good looks like. Someone has to frame the problem, review the output, catch mistakes, understand tradeoffs, and make judgment calls. That usually favors senior talent.

BLS also projects that AI demand will help drive the need for 926,700 new workers in professional, scientific, and technical services, while office and administrative support roles are expected to lose 752,100 jobs as AI and automation reduce demand.
Employers may say they want skills over credentials, but they still use degrees as signals. If the credential changes, companies need to be clearer about what they actually value.
Employees now lose 51 working days a year to technology friction, according to WalkMe's annual State of Digital Adoption 2026. The trend has reversed: 43 days in 2024, 36 in 2025, and now 51 in 2026.
88% of leaders believe their people have adequate tools. Only 21% of employees agree. Executives estimate their organizations run about 35 applications. The actual number is 661.
